formulations.label: Chewable tablets 1500 mg (calcium only, no vitamin D)
formulations.strengths: Calcium carbonate 1500 mg (600 mg elemental calcium) per tablet
formulations.note: This entry covers the calcium-only product. Calcium carbonate products that also contain colecalciferol (vitamin D3) are different medicines and are not covered here.

src.q: Calcium carbonate: 1500mg equivalent to 600mg of elemental calcium
1. Name of the medicinal product Adcal 1500mg Chewable Tablets

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Supplementary source of calcium when requirements are high, and correction of dietary calcium deficiency.

src.q: recommended as a supplementary source of calcium when normal requirements are high and in the correction of calcium deficiency in the diet

items.t: Adjunct to specific osteoporosis treatments.

src.q: They can be used in osteoporosis therapy as an adjunct to more specific conventional treatments.

items.t: Phosphate binder in renal failure.

src.q: Adcal chewable tablets can be used as a phosphate binding agent in the management of renal failure.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restrictions in the calcium carbonate SmPC.

items.t: Adults and elderly: 2 chewable tablets per day (each tablet 600 mg elemental calcium), preferably one in the morning and one in the evening.

src.q: Dietary deficiency and as an adjunct in osteoporosis therapy; 2 chewable tablets per day, preferably one tablet each morning and evening.
equivalent to 600mg of elemental calcium

items.t: Dose adjusted for the individual patient according to serum phosphate.

src.q: For use in binding phosphate in the management of renal failure in patients on renal dialysis, the dose should be adjusted for the individual patient and is dependent on the serum phosphate level.

items.t: The SmPC gives the same dose for adults, elderly and children (2 chewable tablets per day) and states no lower age limit.

src.q: Adults, elderly and children Dietary deficiency and as an adjunct in osteoporosis therapy; 2 chewable tablets per day

items.t: Hypercalcaemia (e.g. from myeloma, bone metastases, other malignant bone disease, sarcoidosis).

src.q: Absolute contra-indications are hypercalcaemia resulting for example from myeloma, bone metastases or other malignant bone disease, sarcoidosis

items.t: Primary hyperparathyroidism and vitamin D overdosage.

src.q: primary hyperparathyroidism and vitamin D overdosage

items.t: Severe renal failure not treated by renal dialysis.

src.q: Severe renal failure untreated by renal dialysis.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to any tablet ingredient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to any of the tablet ingredients.

items.t: Relative contraindications: osteoporosis due to prolonged immobilisation, renal stones, severe hypercalciuria.

src.q: Relative contra-indications are osteoporosis due to prolonged immobilisation, renal stones, severe hypercalciuria.

items.t: Mild to moderate renal failure or mild hypercalciuria: supervise carefully and check plasma calcium and urinary calcium excretion periodically.

src.q: Patients with mild to moderate renal failure or mild hypercalciuria should be supervised carefully.
Periodic checks of plasma calcium levels and urinary calcium excretion should be made

items.t: History of renal stones: measure urinary calcium excretion to exclude hypercalciuria.

src.q: In patients with a history of renal stones urinary calcium excretion should be measured to exclude hypercalciuria.

items.t: Allow for calcium and vitamin D from other sources.

src.q: Allowances should be made for calcium and vitamin D supplements from other sources.

items.t: Should not be taken by people with hereditary fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take this medicine.

items.t: Calcium reduces absorption of thyroxine (levothyroxine), quinolones (e.g. ciprofloxacin), tetracyclines, bisphosphonates, sodium fluoride and iron. Calcium carbonate SmPC: allow at least 4 hours before taking the calcium.

src.q: Calcium salts may reduce the absorption of thyroxine, bisphosphonates, sodium fluoride, quinolone and tetracycline antibiotics or iron.
It is advisable to allow a minimum period of four hours before taking the calcium.

items.t: Levothyroxine SmPC: calcium salts and antacids may reduce levothyroxine absorption; separate by 4-5 hours.

src.q: Absorption of levothyroxine (thyroxine) possibly reduced by antacids, calcium salts
(administration should be separated by 4-5 hours)

items.t: Ciprofloxacin SmPC: give ciprofloxacin 1-2 hours before or at least 4 hours after calcium-containing products.

src.q: multivalent cation-containing drugs and mineral supplements (e.g. calcium, magnesium, aluminium, iron)
ciprofloxacin should be administered either 1-2 hours before or at least 4 hours after these preparations

items.t: Hydroxychloroquine SmPC: antacids may reduce hydroxychloroquine absorption; keep a 4-hour interval.

src.q: antacids may reduce absorption of hydroxychloroquine so it is advised that a 4 hour interval be observed between hydroxychloroquine sulfate and antacid dosing

items.t: Iron: if both are needed, take at different times.

src.q: If Adcal and iron supplements are both required to be administered to the patient, they should be taken at different times

items.t: Thiazide diuretics reduce urinary calcium excretion: consider the risk of hypercalcaemia.

src.q: The risk of hypercalcaemia should be considered in patients taking thiazide diuretics since these drugs can reduce urinary calcium excretion.

items.t: Digitalis/cardiac glycosides: avoid hypercalcaemia; strict medical supervision and, if needed, ECG and calcium monitoring.

src.q: Hypercalcaemia must be avoided in digitalised patients.
Strict medical supervision is needed and, if necessary monitoring of ECG and calcium.

items.t: Systemic corticosteroids reduce calcium absorption.

src.q: Calcium absorption is reduced in patients receiving systemic corticosteroid therapy.

items.t: Foods containing oxalic acid, phosphate or phytinic acid may reduce calcium absorption.

src.q: Certain foods (e.g. those containing oxalic acid, phosphate or phytinic acid) may reduce the absorption of calcium

items.t: Contraindicated in severe renal failure not treated by dialysis.

src.q: Severe renal failure untreated by renal dialysis.

items.t: Mild to moderate renal failure: supervise carefully; check plasma calcium and urinary calcium periodically. (No eGFR/CrCl thresholds given.)

src.q: Patients with mild to moderate renal failure or mild hypercalciuria should be supervised carefully.

items.t: On renal dialysis: can be used as a phosphate binder, dose by serum phosphate.

src.q: the dose should be adjusted for the individual patient and is dependent on the serum phosphate level

hepatic.note: No hepatic impairment advice in the calcium carbonate SmPC.

items.t: Use in pregnancy under the direction of a physician. Calcium needs are higher; allow for calcium from other sources.

src.q: During pregnancy and lactation treatment with Adcal should be under the direction of a physician.
allowances should be made for availability of these agents from other sources

items.t: Calcium carbonate SmPC: use during lactation under the direction of a physician.

src.q: During pregnancy and lactation treatment with Adcal should be under the direction of a physician.

items.t: SPS: calcium carbonate can be used during breastfeeding at the doses used for heartburn and dyspepsia; no specific infant monitoring usually needed (calcium is a natural part of breast milk, poor oral bioavailability).

src.q: Calcium carbonate can be used during breastfeeding at recommended doses used for heartburn and dyspepsia
calcium is a natural component of breast milk

reproductive.note: No fertility or contraception statements in the calcium carbonate SmPC.

items.t: No common or very common effects listed. Rarely: mild GI upset (constipation, flatulence, nausea, gastric pain, diarrhoea).

src.q: The use of calcium supplements has, rarely, given rise to mild gastro-intestinal disturbances, such as constipation, flatulence, nausea, gastric pain, diarrhoea.

items.t: Hypercalcaemia is not expected from overdose except with excessive vitamin D; treat by lowering serum calcium (high fluid intake, low calcium diet).

src.q: would not be expected to cause hypercalcaemia except in patients treated with excessive doses of vitamin D
Treatment should be aimed at lowering serum calcium levels through a high fluid intake and low calcium diet.

items.t: History of renal stones: measure urinary calcium excretion before treatment to exclude hypercalciuria.

src.q: In patients with a history of renal stones urinary calcium excretion should be measured to exclude hypercalciuria.

items.t: Long-term treatment: monitor serum and urinary calcium and kidney function. Mild to moderate renal failure or mild hypercalciuria: periodic plasma and urinary calcium.

src.q: With long-term treatment it is advisable to monitor serum and urinary calcium levels and kidney function

items.t: Reduce or stop treatment temporarily if urinary calcium exceeds 7.5 mmol/24 hours.

src.q: reduce or stop treatment temporarily if urinary calcium exceeds 7.5mmol/24 hours

items.t: Chew the tablets (do not swallow whole). Take just before, during or immediately after a meal.

src.q: The tablets should be chewed, not swallowed whole and taken just prior to, during or immediately following a meal.

items.t: Chew each tablet with a meal; usual dose one in the morning and one in the evening.

src.q: preferably one tablet each morning and evening

items.t: Take levothyroxine, quinolone antibiotics, tetracyclines, bisphosphonates or iron first and wait at least 4 hours before taking calcium.

src.q: It is advisable to allow a minimum period of four hours before taking the calcium.

items.t: Tell the prescriber about other calcium or vitamin D supplements.

src.q: Allowances should be made for calcium and vitamin D supplements from other sources.
